description: The Simple Moving Average (SMA) calculates the arithmetic mean of log returns over the last intervals. It is used to smooth out price data and identify the underlying market trend. While the SMA over the last 20 intervals captures short-term trends within the 5-minute resolution, an SMA over the last 200 intervals serves as an indicators for medium- and long-term momentum.
Logarithmic returns are calculated as the natural log difference of successive prices. Different prices in the horizons capture the dynamics of the returns respectively.

Applying a logarithmic transformation to trading volume reduces the skewness of the data, as volume often exhibits extreme spikes. It serves as an indicator of market activity and liquidity. An increase in log-volume validates the significance of a price movement, helping the model distinguish between meaningful market entries and random noise.
The Exponential Moving Average (EMA) applies more weight to recent data points. Compared to the SMA, the EMA reacts more quickly to abrupt price changes.

Kurtosis measures the tailedness of the return distribution over a set rolling interval window. In financial analysis, high kurtosis indicates a higher probability of extreme events. This feature can inform the model whether the market is in a stable state or if the risk of outliers is currently increased.

On-Balance Volume is a cumulative momentum indicator that relates volume to price change. It adds volume of the current interval when the current close price is higher than the previous close price otherwise it is subtracted.

This categorical feature identifies the specific trading day (Monday-Friday) numericaly. It allows the model to potentially learn temporal patterns (lower returns on specific days, volatility patterns occurring at the beginning or end of the trading week).

This feature encodes the intra-day time component numericaly. In high-frequency 5-minute data, this can be helpful for learning time-of-day specific behaviors, such as high-volatility patterns during market open and close.

The daily close provides a more stable level of close price. It represents the last interval's close price of the previous trading day. The value could influence the opening sentiment of the current intervals opening day.
A volume spike is calculated as the ratio of current volume to its moving average over n-periods.

The volume ratio compares a short-term (fast) moving average of volume to a long-term (slow) moving average. It acts as a normalized momentum oscillator for market activity. It is more stable to noise than volume spike indicator.
This feature calculates the rolling standard deviation of log returns over various horizons. In a 5-minute context, it can help to understand the current risk environment.
The high-low range measures the maximum price spread (high price minus low price of each interval) over a specific window. It captures the total range covered by the price.
The open-close range measures the absolute distance between the opening- and closing prices of each interval
Turnover represents the total monetary value of shares traded during each interval.
The Relative Strength Index (RSI) is a bounded oscillator that measures the speed and change of price movements.

The price Rate of Change (ROC) is a momentum oscillator that measures the percentage change between the current price and the price n-periods ago. It quantifies the velocity of the trend. Positive ROC values indicate an accelerating uptrend, while negative values signal a strengthening downtrend
The Average Directional Index (ADX) quantifies trend strength without regard to direction.

The Vortex Indicator (VI) consists of two lines (VI+ and VI-) that capture positive and negative trend movement. It is designed to identify the start of a new trend and its direction by measuring the distance between price extremes.
The Directional Movement Index (DMI) consists of DI+ and DI- which help to identify the direction of the trend. When +DI is above -DI, the upward pressure dominates.

The Commodity Channel Index (CCI) measures the current price relative to an average price over a given period. High values indicate that prices are unusually high compared to the average, while low values indicate they are unusually low.
The Mass Index (MI) examines the range between high and low prices over time. It is used to predict trend reversals by analyzing the movement of the price range.
The Stochastic Oscillator (STOCH) presents the location of the close price relative to the high-low  price range over a specific number of periods. It follows the speed or momentum of price.
Percent Bandwidth (%B) quantifies the price relationship to the Bollinger Bands. A value of 1.0 means the price is at the upper band, while 0.0 means it is at the lower band.

The Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) is a trend-following momentum indicator that shows the relationship between two moving averages of the close price. It consists of the MACD line (difference between 12 and 26-period EMAs close price) and a signal line (9-period EMA of the MACD line). Crossovers between these lines help the model identify shifts in trend direction.

The Percentage Volume Oscillator (PVO) is the volume-based equivalent of the MACD. It measures the difference between a fast and a slow EMA of volume. It allows the model to identify whether volume is increasing or decreasing relative to the long-term average.
The Normalized Average True Range (NATR) is a measure of volatility that is normalized by the closing price.
The Money Flow Index (MFI) is a technical oscillator that uses both price and volume to measure buying and selling pressure.
